input:
This case considers the inventory policy for a spare motor and the question of how much safety stock should be held to protect availability. The bottom-line recommendation is that safety stock for the spare motor should be set at 785 units, a figure designed to deliver a 95% cycle service level given mean demand of 1668 units per week, a standard deviation of 238 units per week, and a replenishment lead time of 4 weeks.

Safety stock fulfils a specific and important function within the policy: because demand during the lead time fluctuates around its mean, the stock is held to absorb that fluctuation and prevent a stockout before the next replenishment delivery arrives. The three inputs together determine the scale of the fluctuation that the stock is required to absorb. Demand averages some 1668 units per week, the week-to-week standard deviation stands at 238 units, and a replenishment order takes 4 weeks to arrive. The service level, in turn, determines how much of that fluctuation the stock is expected to cover: a 95% cycle service level consciously accepts that a stockout will occur in the remaining cycles, rather than holding stock for the largest demand the distribution could generate.

The reorder point can be derived from exactly the same set of inputs. Mean demand over the 4-week lead time amounts to 1668 x 4 = 6672 units, and once safety stock is added, the reorder point becomes 6672 + 785 = 7065 units.

The policy proceeds on the basis that demand is normally distributed and independent from week to week. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the demand figures, which means that the 785 units have not been sized with seasonal peaks in mind, and any peak falling within a lead time will draw on stock the calculation did not set aside for it. Within these parameters, the figure is fully determined by the inputs as stated: mean demand of 1668 units per week, a standard deviation of 238 units, a lead time of 4 weeks, and a 95% cycle service level together give a safety stock of 785 units.
